brave-llmcontext.title: E337
brave-llmcontext.snippet:
E337 potassium sodium tartrate, also called Rochelle salt, is a stabiliser and acidity regulator considered safe at normal permitted food-use levels.
### Common uses and where E337 appears
E337 may be used as a stabiliser, sequestrant, emulsifier, or pH-control agent in selected foods including cheese products, processed fruit, confectionery, and other regulated categories.
## Common uses of E337 – Potassium sodium tartrate food additive
- **Cheese and cheese products:** It can function as an emulsifier or pH-control agent in permitted formulations.
- **Jams, jellies, and fruit preparations:** It may help control acidity or support product stability where permitted.
- **Confectionery and chewing gum:** EU rules allow tartrates in selected confectionery categories subject to applicable limits.
- **Processed fruit and vegetables:** It may be used in specified categories under numerical EU maximum levels.
## Where is E337 – Potassium sodium tartrate food additive allowed (EU vs US)?
In the EU, E337 remains authorised, with current rules placing E334–337 and E354 in the tartaric acid–tartrates group and applying category-specific maximum levels from 16 December 2024. In the US, sodium potassium tartrate is affirmed as GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) for direct food use under good manufacturing practice as an emulsifier and pH-control agent.
## Should You Avoid E337 – Potassium sodium tartrate food additive?
Most people do not need to avoid foods solely because they contain E337 within permitted conditions. Toxicology is broadly reassuring, while the strongest adverse findings involve different tartrate stereoisomers or exposures far above normal food use. Concentrated tartrate salts and laxative-scale doses are not equivalent to ordinary food-additive exposure. Dedicated reproductive-toxicity data are missing, but the reviewed evidence does not identify a specific pregnancy or fertility hazard at normal dietary exposure.

 Potassium acid tartrate is a crystalline chemical compound defined as the potassium acid salt of l‑(+)-tartaric acid, identified by the CAS number 868‑14‑4. It is also commonly called potassium bitartrate or cream of tartar, and it belongs to a class of food additives used for multiple technical functions including acting as an emulsifier and pH control agent in food formulations. As a salt derived from a naturally occurring organic acid found in grapes, it manifests as a white or colorless crystalline powder with a mildly acidic taste, and it has been utilized in food processing and culinary applications for many decades. Under regulatory systems such as the US Code of Federal Regulations, it is recognized as an affirmed generally recognized as safe (GRAS) direct food substance, subject to specifications for purity that ensure it meets food‑grade quality standards. Its diverse nomenclature reflects a range of functional and chemical descriptors used in industry and scientific literature.

 Potassium acid tartrate is used in food production because of its versatile technological functionality and compatibility with food ingredients. Its acidic nature allows it to act as a pH control agent in formulations where specific acidity levels are desired for texture, stability, or microbial control. In baked goods, it is a classic acid component of leavening systems such as baking powder, where it reacts with alkaline bicarbonates to generate carbon dioxide gas and contribute to rise and texture. Its emulsifying and stabilizing properties help maintain the consistency of products like whipped creams and egg white foams, while its buffering capacity supports the maintenance of a controlled acidity environment in confectionery and dairy systems. These combined roles support manufacturability, product consistency, and sensory qualities in a wide range of culinary applications without imparting strong sensory characteristics of its own.

ceramic.title: E337 – Potassium Sodium Tartrate | ohmygoods.app
ceramic.snippet:
E337, known as Potassium Sodium Tartrate, is a double salt of tartaric acid, commonly referred to as Rochelle salt. It functions as an acidity regulator, stabilizer, and sequestrant in various food products.

  Potassium Sodium Tartrate is safe for children when consumed within recommended dietary limits. It contributes to the palatability of various food products, encouraging the consumption of fruit-flavored items.

  Potassium Sodium Tartrate has a slightly salty taste. In food products, it is used to balance flavors without imparting significant off-tastes.

  Potassium Sodium Tartrate is compatible with various food additives and ingredients, making it versatile in food processing. It can be used alongside other acidity regulators, stabilizers, and preservatives to achieve desired product qualities.

  Tartaric acid, from which Potassium Sodium Tartrate is derived, occurs naturally in many plants, especially in grapes. During prolonged storage of wine, a sediment of potassium tartrate, known as tartar, forms in barrels and bottles. This sediment serves as the starting substance for the chemical production of tartaric acid (E334) and its salts, including Potassium Sodium Tartrate (E337).

  • Sodium Tartrates (E335): Used similarly but contain sodium instead of potassium. • Potassium Tartrates (E336): Serve as acidity regulators and can also provide potassium fortification. • Citric Acid (E330): A common acidity regulator and flavoring agent.

  Potassium Sodium Tartrate (E337) is approved for use as a food additive in many countries, including those in the European Union and the United States. Regulatory agencies have established acceptable daily intake levels to ensure consumer safety. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has established a group acceptable daily intake (ADI) for tartaric acid and its salts, including Potassium Sodium Tartrate, of 240 mg/kg body weight per day, expressed as tartaric acid.

# Tartaric Acid

### What is Tartaric Acid?

Tartaric acid is an organic acid that is a by-product of winemaking. It is characterized by its sharp tart taste. In cakes and sweet baked goods production, tartaric acid is used as a fast-acting leavening acid in some baking powders.

As a food acid regulator, it can enhance the profile of fruit flavors and colors and stabilize batter systems. Its salt form, potassium acid tartrate, is commonly known as cream of tartar.

Alternative forms of tartaric acid include:

- Potassium bitartrate
- Sodium potassium tartrate
- Sodium tartrate
...
Tartaric acid is a natural acid which is widely distributed in nature in the form of 2 stereoisomers. It was first isolated by the alchemist Jabir Ibn Hayyan in Iraq in the 7th century. Resolving tartaric acid stereoisomers was done much later by Louis Pasteur in the 1840s.

Similar to other organic compounds such as citric, acetic and lactic acids, tartaric acid has one unreacted carboxyl group (COOH).

### Function

- Flavour enhancer (particularly in lime and grape-flavored beverages)
- Chemical leavener
- Anti-caking agent
- Firming agent
- Humectant
- Acidulant (helps reduce the pH of wine or juice, but not below pH 3.0)
- Antimicrobial or pH control agent, although to a lower extent than citric and other food acids
- Formulation and processing aid

### Commercial production

Tartaric acid can be produced by natural and synthetic routes. The natural route involves the recovery of the reddish precipitated salt, potassium bitartrate, from argol, the sediment in wine vats. The synthetic chemical route involves the production of the racemic mixture of tartaric acid from maleic anhydride.

Commercially, tartaric acid is available as a colorless to white translucent fine crystals or granular crystalline powder. Due to its very high melting point (170°C), tartaric acid is a solid material under room conditions of temperature and pressure.1

exa.title: Sodium Potassium Tartrate Food Additive Reference
exa.snippet:
**Sodium Potassium Tartrate** is a crystalline salt derived from tartaric acid used in food processing for its capacity to act as an emulsifier salt, pH control agent, and sequestrant. It is recognized by regulators in multiple jurisdictions and appears on food additive lists where it supports stability and texture.

...

Sodium Potassium Tartrate is a double salt of tartaric acid, consisting of both sodium and potassium ions bound to the tartrate anion. In food science terms, this substance functions primarily as an emulsifier salt, a pH control agent, and a sequestrant, which means it helps bind metal ions that might otherwise catalyze undesirable reactions in food systems.

...

## Why It Is Used In Food

Food formulators rely on Sodium Potassium Tartrate for multiple technological roles in processed foods. An important function is its capacity to act as a sequestrant, which means it preferentially binds trace metal ions such as iron and copper that can catalyze oxidative reactions or cause color and flavor instability in food products. By complexing these metal ions, the additive helps protect the organoleptic quality of foods over shelf life and prevents undesirable discoloration or off-notes that might otherwise arise from metal-catalyzed reactions. Another key role is pH control. Food systems often require precise acid-base balance to maintain texture, stability, and microbial safety. Sodium Potassium Tartrate contributes buffering capacity that can moderate changes in pH during production, storage, or consumption. This buffering property also supports consistent performance of other additives and ingredients whose functionality is pH dependent. In emulsified products, the compound assists in maintaining stable dispersions of oil and water phases, thereby enhancing texture and preventing phase separation.

## Quick analysis summary about E337 – Potassium sodium tartrate food additive

### Bottom line about E337

E337 is potassium sodium tartrate, also called Rochelle salt. It is graded GREEN – SAFE because evidence does not show a credible concern at permitted food-use levels.

### Why this grade for E337

Long-term L(+)-tartrate evidence is reassuring, direct bacterial testing of E337 was negative, and EFSA exposure estimates remained below its group intake limit.

### Who may want to limit or avoid E337

Most people do not need to avoid E337, although unusually high tartrate intake can have laxative gastrointestinal effects.

### Common uses and where E337 appears

E337 may be used as a stabiliser, sequestrant, emulsifier, or pH-control agent in selected foods including cheese products, processed fruit, confectionery, and other regulated categories.

### E337 source or origin

Commercial E337 is commonly produced from wine-industry tartrate materials and then purified and crystallised, although manufacturing routes can vary.

### Intake note for E337

EFSA set a group ADI (Acceptable Daily Intake) of 240 mg/kg body weight per day, expressed as tartaric acid, while JECFA retains a more conservative group ADI of 0–30 mg/kg body weight per day.

E337 is authorised in the EU and permitted for food use in the US. Japan has treated potassium sodium tartrate as an undesignated additive in import enforcement, which is a non-approval status rather than a toxicity ban.

Sodium tartrate is generally recognized as safe (GRAS) as a direct human food ingredient. It acts as an emulsifier and pH control agent in food products.
Detailed article on Sodium Potassium Tartrate (Rochelle Salt), covering its preparation, properties, structure, and uses. Get information on its chemical formula, and frequently asked questions.
Sodium potassium tartrate is a complex salt of tartaric acid with a chemical formula C 4 H 4 O 6 KNa·4H 2 O . It is also referred to as Rochelle salt or Potassium sodium tartrate . It appears as a colourless to white crystalline powder and has a cool and saline taste. With a pH range of 6.5 – 8.5 , it demonstrates a significant piezometric effect, making it a valuable ingredient in sensitive vibrational and acoustic devices.
Sodium potassium tartrate is used as a laxative . It is employed in the creation of mirror silvering. It is a component in Fehling’s solution. It is utilized in the electroplating process. It is incorporated in cigarette paper manufacturing. It is used to break up emulsions . It is a component in Biuret reagent used to measure protein concentration. It assists in maintaining alkaline pH.
Sodium tartrate is a white, crystalline powder, used as an emulsifier and a binding agent. It can be used in jellies, cheeses, sausage casings and any foods which contain fats or oils.

**FAQ’S**  
**What is Sodium potassium tartrate?**  
Sodium potassium tartrate, also known as Rochelle salt, is a colorless crystals or white crystalline powder that is used in a variety of applications.  
**How is Sodium potassium tartrate made?**  
Sodium potassium tartrate is made by reacting sodium hydroxide with cream of tartar, a by-product of the wine industry.  
**What are the uses of Sodium potassium tartrate?**  
Sodium potassium tartrate is used in consumer electronics (crystal phonograph cartridges, microphones, and earpieces)due to its piezoelectricity. It is used in sensitive devices due to its large piezometric effect. It is used in electroplating that increases cathode efficiency. It is used as an usual precipitant in protein crystallography. It is used as an ingredient in Biuret reagent and Fehling’s solution.  
**How is Sodium potassium tartrate used in Food Industry?**  
Sodium potassium tartrate is used as an emulsifier and pH control agent. It is commonly used in products like cheese, cheese spreads, jellies, and sausage casings. It can also be used in baking powders and leavening agents.

Sodium potassium tartrate (E337)

Potassium sodium tartrate (E337) – what is it?

Potassium sodium tartrate is a salt of tartaric acid, which is a mixture of potassium tartrate and sodium tartrate.

Properties of potassium sodium tartrate

It is a white crystalline powder with the properties of an acidity regulator and anti-caking agent.

Uses of sodium potassium tartrate

It is used in the food industry as an additive to regulate acidity and prevent clumping of ingredients.

Where to buy potassium sodium tartrate?

Potassium sodium tartrate is available in grocery stores, online stores and wholesalers of raw materials for food production.

Potassium sodium tartrate and its functions in food

As a food additive, sodium potassium tartrate helps maintain the stability and quality of food products, improving their appearance and texture.

seltz.snippet:
##### What is tartaric acid?

Tartaric acid is an organic acid that is a by-product of winemaking. It is characterized by its sharp tart taste. In cakes and sweet baked goods production, tartaric acid is used as a fast-acting leavening acid in some baking powders.

As a food acid regulator, it can enhance the profile of fruit flavors and colors and stabilize batter systems. Its salt form, potassium acid tartrate, is commonly known as cream of tartar.

Alternative forms of tartaric acid include:

- Potassium bitartrate
- Sodium potassium tartrate
- Sodium tartrate

### Origin

Tartaric acid is a natural acid which is widely distributed in nature in the form of 2 stereoisomers. It was first isolated by the alchemist Jabir Ibn Hayyan in Iraq in the 7th century. Resolving tartaric acid stereoisomers was done much later by Louis Pasteur in the 1840s.

Similar to other organic compounds such as citric, acetic and lactic acids, tartaric acid has one unreacted carboxyl group (COOH).

### **Function**

- Flavor enhancer (particularly in lime and grape-flavored beverages)
- Chemical leavener
- Anti-caking agent
- Firming agent
- Humectant
- Acidulant (helps reduce the pH of wine or juice, but not below pH 3.0)
- Antimicrobial or pH control agent, although to a lower extent than citric and other food acids
- Formulation and processing aid

### Commercial production

Tartaric acid can be produced by natural and synthetic routes. The natural route involves the recovery of the reddish precipitated salt, potassium bitartrate, from argol, the sediment in wine vats. The synthetic chemical route involves the production of the racemic mixture of tartaric acid from maleic anhydride.

Commercially, tartaric acid is available as a colorless to white translucent fine crystals or granular crystalline powder. Due to its very high melting point (170°C), tartaric acid is a solid material under room conditions of temperature

"Acidulant" is a toolbox, not one ingredient: each acid delivers a different flavor, acid strength, and physical form, so the right one depends on the job - clean citrus tartness, high dry-mix acid strength, mild liquid tang, or pH buffering - not just on hitting a pH number.

By RawSource Editorial

Commercial & Sourcing Desk

7 min read

Getting pH right in a food or beverage is rarely about one number. The same target pH can be reached with a sharp mineral acid, a soft dairy-style acid or a slow-dissolving dry acid — and each tastes, dissolves and behaves differently on the line.

| Formulation goal | Chemistry | Why it works |

**Acidity regulators**, also known as pH control agents, are additives used in processed foods to modify or stabilize their acidity or alkalinity, which is measured by the pH value. Their function often overlaps with that of other food additives: some can also act as preservatives, others as emulsifiers, while some help preserve the color of the food to which they are added. In this way, they contribute, along with other factors, to maintaining or improving the organoleptic properties of the product.[1][2]

Like other food additives, acidity regulators are identified both by their chemical name and by the **E-numbering system**.[3]

According to the scientific evidence currently available, when used in accordance with specific guidelines, acidity regulators are not harmful to human health.[4][5]
